newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury sees need to clarify derivatives law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury sees need to clarify derivatives law.

text.p: A U.S. Treasury Department official reiterated Friday the need for new legislation that would resolve uncertainty about the scope of a legal amendment governing certain types of derivatives transactions.

The Treasury amendment of 1974 was meant to allow banks and other big dealers to keeping trading such instruments as foreign exchange forward contracts outside the expanded reach of futures regulation.
"It has historically been Treasury's position that legislation is needed," Deputy Treasury Secretary Roger Anderson told a futures and securites industry conference.

Anderson said the amendment, part of a broad U.S. law covering commodity futures trading, needs to be changed so that it clearly gives futures regulators the authority to police certain foreign exchange market deals.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has maintained that the amendment already gives it jurisdiction to do so. But Anderson raised questions about whether the futures regulatory agency has any authority over foreign exchange transactions.
The uncertainty has dogged the market and drew harsh criticism last month from the General Accounting Office, the auditing arm of Congress.

Indiana Republican Richard Lugar and Vermont Democrat Patrick Leahy offered a bill early this week that would modify the current law governing futures markets. They characterized the proposal as a starting point for reforming laws next year.
The lawmakers have given the Treasury and the CFTC until the end of this year to reach an agreement on how the Treasury amendment should be interpreted.

"I think we have a good chance of coming to agreement on it," Anderson said. He maintained that an upcoming Supreme Court case on one interpretation of the amendment "won't answer all the uncertainties" or deal with all the issues.
